claims.text: The initial TiVNbTa alloy is a single-phase, dendritic BCC material.
The TiVNbTa alloy has a low-temperature yield strength of approximately 800 MPa.
At 1273 K, the TiVNbTa alloy has a yield strength of approximately 330 MPa.
At 1273 K and 30% strain, the TiVNbTa alloy has a compressive strength of approximately 423 MPa.
A controlled heat treatment can induce a fine secondary precipitate phase in TiVNbTa.
The induced precipitates can be nanoscale and uniformly dispersed within the BCC matrix.
TiO is a candidate strengthening precipitate for the proposed intervention.
A Laves phase is a candidate strengthening precipitate for the proposed intervention.
The precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion and provide precipitation strengthening.
The precipitates will impede grain-boundary sliding and creep.
The precipitates will remain stable enough at approximately 1273 K to mitigate high-temperature strength loss.
The treated alloy will have a yield strength above the untreated baseline of approximately 330 MPa at 1273 K.
The treated alloy will have improved compressive strength at 1273 K relative to untreated TiVNbTa.
The treated alloy will retain sufficient ductility for use as a W–CuCrZr intermediate layer.
The relevant boundary conditions are approximately 1273 K under tensile or compressive loading to roughly 30–40% strain.
Those temperature and strain conditions represent the requirements of a thermally stressed intermediate layer between tungsten and CuCrZr.
The optimal precipitate identity, size, and distribution are not yet defined.
Precipitate stability at 1273 K and the effect of precipitation on thermal conductivity remain uncertain.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes the heat treatment as producing a fine, stable secondary phase, while the uncertainty field states that precipitate stability at 1273 K has not been established.
